source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: Five frontier models were asked to answer medical multiple-choice items where the correct option had been removed. They still picked an answer most of the time, even though abstaining was allowed. A short safety prompt cut this by about a third but did not remove it.
numbers: MedQA n=500 (250 intact, 250 no-correct-option); AfriMed-QA n=490. Baseline false-action rate averaged about 70% on both; 55-81% (MedQA) and 53-82% (AfriMed) across models. With safety prompt about 48% on both. Claude Opus 4.7 highest (81% to 65% on MedQA). Grok 3 dropped 75% to 29% but lost accuracy on intact items; the other four models lost about 1.0 point on intact items.
limits: Premature closure here means answering when abstention was right, not holding too few hypotheses. Model names as reported by the authors. Mean intact-accuracy loss excludes Grok 3.
agent_relevance: A model will commit to one of the listed options even when none fits. Our agent should keep an explicit 'none of these / hypothesis set incomplete' slot that code checks. A prompt alone only half fixes it (G1, G3).

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs (open-ended part)
finding: On open-ended health questions, models closed early most often when the case was underspecified but looked harmless. They were much better when urgency cues were explicit. So the models react to danger cues, not to missing information.
numbers: HealthBench subset n=861: overall premature closure 20.7% (GPT-5.4) to 44.6% (DeepSeek R1). Underspecified low-risk items: 73.2% to 96.1%, average 81%. Underspecified urgent items: 5.0% to 35.8%, average 19%. Safety prompt cut overall rates by 4.2-7.9 points. Adversarial n=191: 59.3% to 91.4% at baseline; lowest after safety prompt 50.8% (Claude Opus 4.7). Sufficient-context control: clarification rate 3.5% under both prompts, so no broad over-deferral.
limits: Graded against physician rubrics by a model-based grader; five models only; one safety-prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Premature closure is worst when nothing signals trouble. Doubt should be triggered by a measured information gap (a discriminating test not yet run), not by perceived risk. Supports G1 with the signal defined by code.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: 32 models had to ask for clinical data one item at a time over three rounds. Differential reasoning was the weakest part for every one of the 32 models. Models asked for less data as rounds went on and stopped searching early.
numbers: 20 hematologic cancer cases, 32 models. Best overall 68.1% (Claude Opus 4.6); mean 56.3 +/- 7.4. Diagnosis 66.6%, treatment 58.8%, differential 43.6%; gap between diagnosis and differential 23.0 points on average. Requests per round 7.5, 4.2, 1.8. Share of available data obtained 56.8%, 56.7%, 25.7%. Utilization vs accuracy R=0.69, p<0.001.
limits: Judged by an LLM judge checked against one hematologist; differential score is the most subjective part; one specialty; not all models finished all cases.
agent_relevance: Models name a likely answer but do not weigh rivals, and they stop gathering evidence before the discriminating data. The program should count how many hypotheses are alive and how much discriminating evidence was requested before S7 select.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) OncoRounds: anchoring and error taxonomy
finding: Early wrong diagnoses were sticky. Early right diagnoses were often lost later. Annotated reasoning traces showed search satisficing, premature closure and anchoring as the top errors.
numbers: 630 model-case pairs with round-1 and round-3 diagnoses. Of 323 with wrong or partial round-1 diagnosis, 212 (65.6%) stayed wrong (recovery 34.4%). Of 307 correct at round 1, 156 (50.8%) fell to wrong or partial by round 3. Recovery ranged from 100% (Claude Opus 4.5, 6 of 6) to 7.1% (Qwen3 Next 80B, 1 of 14). Errors in 89 of 1008 evaluations (8.8%); 93 annotations across 17 models; 60.2% medium severity. Reasoning rubric 91% above threshold but decorrelated from accuracy.
limits: Anchoring was mostly at the level of diagnostic resolution (e.g. disease family), not a specific wrong disease. Error annotation was done on traces, which G10 says are weak evidence of cause.
agent_relevance: Fluent reasoning does not predict correct hypotheses. Re-opening the hypothesis set after new data should be forced by code when findings contradict the leader, since recovery from an early error is about one in three.

source: Wang (2026) Measuring the Unmeasurable: a diagnostic sensor for AI reasoning pathology in sequential clinical decision-making (medRxiv)
finding: When case information arrived in stages, Claude Sonnet 4 sometimes reached the right diagnosis mid-way and then dropped it. A scaffold that forced tracking of hypotheses removed those drops, but top-1 accuracy fell.
numbers: 50 case reports, 3 conditions, 150 runs; deep analysis on 10 cases. Unscaffolded sequential: correct diagnosis reached in 9/10 but kept in final output in 6/10 (convergence regression in 3/10). Scaffolded (SIPS): access 80%, final top-3 80%, 0 regressions in 40 stage observations, top-1 60% to 40%, hypothesis tracking 4.10 to 4.70, anchoring resistance 3.33 to 4.13 (5-point scale), output tokens +28%.
limits: Single author, LLM-assisted scoring, no inter-rater check, tiny sample, no statistical tests, one main model, preprint. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: A tracked-hypothesis scaffold trades top-1 for keeping the right answer in the top 3. Our program should hold the full list and promote on evidence, and report top-k and top-1 separately. Treat as a lead, not proof.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: One model role-playing a panel that includes a hypothesis tracker (top-three differential with probabilities) and a challenger that looks for anchoring and disconfirming tests did better than the same base model without it.
numbers: 304 NEJM cases (56 hidden test). Physicians 19.9% at $2,963. o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO on o3: 81.9% at $4,735 (no budget), 79.9% at about $2,396 (budgeted), 85.5% ensemble. GPT-4o 49.3%. Batched vs single testing both 83.9% on test set. Roles: Dr. Hypothesis, Test-Chooser, Challenger, Stewardship, Checklist.
limits: No per-role ablation, so the anchoring challenger's own contribution is not isolated. Anchoring and premature-closure claims are qualitative. Physicians were not allowed outside resources. Page read through a summarizer.
agent_relevance: A method from this subfield already used in an LLM loop: explicit top-3 differential plus a falsification role. Our G4 and G9 warn that persona panels are correlated, so test whether the gain comes from the hypothesis list and disconfirming-test step (keep) or from the personas (drop).

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning, but GPT-4 alone scored higher than both physician groups. The score covered the differential, factors for and against each hypothesis, and next steps.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), up to 6 vignettes in 60 minutes. Median score 76% (IQR 66-87) with LLM vs 74% (63-84) conventional; adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60). Median time per case 519 s with LLM; difference -82 s (95% CI -195 to 31, p=.20). LLM alone 16 points higher than conventional group (95% CI 2-30, p=.03).
limits: Physicians had little prompt training; LLM-alone arm was a secondary comparison; one model; vignettes only.
agent_relevance: Handing a human the LLM's differential did not help; the human still has to weigh it. For our agent, a hypothesis list only helps if code makes it drive the next test, not if it is just shown as text.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards Accurate Differential Diagnosis with Large Language Models
finding: A tuned LLM produced a differential list alone and as an aid. Clinicians helped by it gave more complete lists than clinicians alone or with search.
numbers: 302 NEJM cases, 20 clinicians. Top-10 accuracy: LLM alone 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6% (p=0.04). Clinicians with LLM 51.7% vs 36.1% without (McNemar p<0.01); with search 44.4% (p=0.03).
limits: Abstract page read through a summarizer only; list length not given. Specialised model, not off-the-shelf. Top-10 is a lenient measure.
agent_relevance: Machine-generated lists widened the set of hypotheses people considered. Unlike c07, here the aid helped, so the effect depends on task and scoring (list breadth vs reasoning quality). Breadth by sampling many candidates is cheap for the agent (S3).

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview put the correct diagnosis in its differential in most hard cases and beat GPT-4 and attending physicians, especially when little information was available.
numbers: NEJM CPCs: correct diagnosis in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8); first suggestion correct 52%. On 70 cases shared with a GPT-4 study: exact or very close 88.6% vs 72.9% (p=.015). ER study, 79 cases, three touchpoints: o1 exact or very close 65.8%, 69.6%, 79.7% vs physician 1 54.4%, 60.8%, 75.9% and physician 2 48.1%, 50.6%, 68.4%. Median share of cannot-miss diagnoses included 0.92.
limits: Retrospective cases; possible training-data overlap (no significant before/after cutoff difference: 79.8% vs 73.5%, p=0.59); text only.
agent_relevance: The gap between 'in the list' (78%) and 'first' (52%) shows list breadth is good but ranking is the weak step. Ranking should be done by code from evidence (G5), not by the model's first guess.

source: Kanjee, Crowe, Rodman (2023) Accuracy of a Generative AI Model in a Complex Diagnostic Challenge (JAMA)
finding: GPT-4 was tested on NEJM clinicopathologic conferences. Its top diagnosis matched the final diagnosis in about 39% and the final diagnosis was somewhere in its differential in about 64%.
numbers: Search-snippet figures: 64% in differential, 39% top; denominator reported as 70 in news and 75 in a preprint, unresolved.
limits: Not opened; denominator conflicts between sources. Use only as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the older GPT-4 level that c09 improves on (72.9% exact or very close on the same 70 cases).

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompting for a differential diagnosis first did not help accuracy on MedQA and hurt the older model. Clinical-reasoning-style prompts gave no reliable gain for GPT-4. One recipe tried was 'list a broad differential of 6, then narrow to 3'.
numbers: GPT-3.5: chain-of-thought 46%, intuitive 48% (p=0.9), analytic 40% (-6, p=0.001), differential diagnosis 38% (-8, p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4, p=0.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78% (+2.2, CI -1.4 to 5.8, p=0.24), analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, p=0.07). Inter-rater kappa 0.93 (GPT-3.5); 99% agreement (GPT-4).
limits: Multiple-choice MedQA, where options are already supplied, so a self-written differential adds little; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only; the 6-to-3 recipe is not scored separately in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to write a differential before answering is not free. At equal tokens it is neutral at best (G7). Breadth should be earned by the test step, not forced by a prompt.

source: BiasMedQA authors (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
finding: One biased sentence added to a USMLE question, pushing toward a wrong answer, lowered accuracy for all six models. Weaker models fell a lot; GPT-4 fell less. Mitigation prompts gave modest gains.
numbers: 1,273 MedQA questions, 7 biases. No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 0.727, Mixtral 0.518, GPT-3.5 0.497, PaLM-2 0.429, Llama 2 70B 0.357, PMC Llama 13B 0.334. False consensus: GPT-4 0.625, GPT-3.5 0.239, Llama 2 0.139. Frequency bias: GPT-4 0.627, PaLM-2 0.167. Average drop largest for false consensus (24.9%), smallest for confirmation (8.1%). GPT-4 education prompt raised the frequency case from 0.627 to 0.720; few-shot GPT-4 range 0.726-0.770.
limits: Per-condition sample sizes not given; paper inconsistent on a model name; one-shot and few-shot no-bias baselines differ from Table 1 (0.763, 0.757) without explanation; PaLM-2 non-response up to 99.5% so excluded.
agent_relevance: A suggested wrong answer in the input anchors models, and bias-awareness prompts only partly undo it. The agent should keep any user-supplied hypothesis separate from the evidence and test it as one candidate, not as the prior.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Models showed anchoring on earlier decisions, framing, primacy and group attribution in a synthetic admissions task. Telling the model to avoid bias worked poorly. Having the model rewrite its own prompt ('selfhelp') worked better, but only the strong models could safely revise.
numbers: 13,465 baseline prompts; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B. GPT-4 admit rate 0.375 under admit framing vs 0.780 under reject framing. Awareness prompt: GPT-4 framing delta worsened to -0.470. Selfhelp left 0% (group attribution) and 2.7% (framing) of biased prompts for GPT-4. Decisions changed when allowed to revise: GPT-3.5 5.2%, GPT-4 17.5%, Llama-2-7B 39.9%, Llama-2-13B 52.1%.
limits: Task is student admissions, not diagnosis; anchoring is an order effect across sequential decisions; contrastive few-shot sometimes collapsed to always-admit.
agent_relevance: Instructions to 'avoid bias' do not remove anchoring (G1). Cleaning the input (removing the anchor) is stronger than asking the model to resist it.

source: Lou, Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: LLM numeric answers shift toward whichever hint is shown. Expert hints pull harder than facts. Four prompt fixes did not remove it. Showing two opposite hints brought answers near the unbiased value for some questions.
numbers: Questions built from a human anchoring dataset. Fact hints: 162 distribution comparisons, only 11 not following the hint direction. 12 of 12 questions with a PTF-expert hint followed the expert. Time-period questions gave 6 of the 11 exceptions. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, ignore-anchor and reflection all left effects with very small p-values. Both-anchors strategy landed near the unbiased value on about 8 of 15 questions (GPT-4).
limits: Numeric estimation, not diagnosis; GPT-family models; effect smaller than in the human study they compare to.
agent_relevance: Showing the model a range of opposing candidates works better than telling it to ignore one. For the agent: present competing hypotheses together, never a single leading one.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: 45 models were tested on 8 cognitive biases with 2.8 million responses. Anchoring resistance was middling and rose with model size, then flattened. Prompt detail helped anchoring most at a moderate level.
numbers: 220 scenarios, 45 LLMs. Bias-consistent behaviour in 17.8-57.3% of instances. Anchoring resistance score (higher is better): 0.49 (DeepSeek-R1-Q-1.5B) to 0.78 (QwQ-32B); Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.563, Qwen2.5-72B 0.761. By prompt detail level: TELeR L1 0.611, L2 0.649 (peak), L3 0.625, L4 0.621, L5 0.643. Models above 32B reduced bias in 39.5% of cases; about 56% of the size gain falls between 0.5B and 32B.
limits: Multiple-choice proxy tasks with fixed answer extraction; not medical; scores are resistance rates, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: More prompt detail is not monotone for anchoring, and resistance does not improve much past about 32B, so a bigger model is not a fix. Structural scaffolds are needed.

source: Jones, Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Using human cognitive biases as hypotheses about model failure found that Codex output shifts toward anchors in the prompt and mimics frequent training examples.
numbers: Abstract page only; no effect sizes on the page I read.
limits: Only the abstract was read; no numbers; code-generation case study.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that anchoring in prompts is a general model property, so any hint in our context (a user guess, an earlier attempt) will pull the next attempt.

source: Mehta, Datta (2026) When Agents Commit Too Soon: Diagnosing Premature Commitment in LLM Agents
finding: Hidden states from repeated ReAct runs become similar early (step 4), and similarity predicts how little the whole run varies. But this measures stability, not correctness: shared evidence explains much of it, it disappears on hard questions, and confidently wrong runs look like correct ones. A prompt telling the agent to commit reduced run variability but not accuracy.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B ReAct on HotpotQA: step-4 similarity vs variability r=-0.35 (95% CI -0.51 to -0.16, p=0.0006). Replicated on two other models (Phi-3 r=-0.36, n=91; another r=-0.65) and StrategyQA. Monitor from three partial runs AUROC 0.81 (bootstrap CI 0.68-0.94). Commitment prompt cut variability 28% vs token-matched filler (d=0.33, Holm p=.003) but only 15% vs standard agent (Holm p=.088, not significant); accuracy not improved (baseline 93.2%).
limits: Needs hidden-state access; HotpotQA accuracy near ceiling; authors state it cannot show that commitment was premature.
agent_relevance: Agreement across runs and early settling are not evidence of being right (G4). A cheap convergence monitor can signal that the hypothesis set has collapsed, which is a trigger for doubt, never a verdict.

source: Lu et al. (2026) Beyond Fault Localization: A Trajectory-Level Study of LLM Agents for Microservice Root Cause Analysis
finding: Across 5,000 agent trajectories, successful investigations used evidence to steer later queries, considered more kinds of diagnostic intent and dug deeper. Failed ones drifted to unrelated services or repeated shallow queries. One named failure was 'anchor lock': an early hypothesis kept despite contradicting evidence.
numbers: 5,000 trajectories, 10 framework-backbone setups on RCABench, 9 frameworks, 2 backbones. Frameworks that fix hypotheses up front or commit early scored lower: GoS 48.2% (fixes hypotheses, three retrieval steps, tests only the most credible), OpenRCA 46.6% (commits as soon as it can answer), mABC 42.6% (no iteration over evidence). Incorrect baseline runs showed 3.29 distinct failure modes on average vs 0.71 for correct runs.
limits: The per-mode prevalence table was hard to read from the PDF text, so anchor-lock prevalence is not recorded. Failure codes assigned by the authors' pipeline.
agent_relevance: Fixing the hypothesis list up front and testing only the leader is a documented loser. The agent should keep a live list and let evidence move the leader.

source: Lu et al. (2026) DiagGuard intervention (same paper, RQ4 and RQ5)
finding: A wrapper with a self-audit before investigation, a soundness check at verdict time, and a step that profiles the search space to surface overlooked axes raised accuracy in all 14 configurations. In the worked example the baseline stayed on a noisy service and never looked at the storage tier; the wrapped agent went down to the infrastructure tier.
numbers: Acc@1 gains +3.5 to +35.1 points; median +10.5 on RCA100 (12 configs); AIOps 2025 +6.5 (Qwen) and +9.0 (Doubao). Ablation on 400 incidents, Doubao, 5 runs: baseline 43.5 +/- 0.6; without Grounder 47.6 (+4.1); without Verifier 48.0 (+4.5); full 52.5 +/- 1.1 (+9.0); cost about $0.16 vs $0.09 per incident. mABC +21.1 and +35.1 from bases of 35.1% and 3.5%.
limits: Authors built DiagGuard from the same failure codes they measured it against; only two backbones; largest gains where the baseline was very low.
agent_relevance: Two code-triggered steps map to our schema: list untried diagnostic axes before the first query (S2/S3) and reconcile the verdict with gathered evidence (S8). Gains were additive, supporting keeping both.

source: Bai et al. (2025) FVDebug: An LLM-Driven Debugging Assistant for Automated Root Cause Analysis of Formal Verification Failures
finding: A hardware-debug agent keeps one hypothesis per suspicious node, each with narrative, evidence, confidence score and an unexplored frontier. Weak hypotheses are marked but kept for the final report. A for-and-against prompt analyses each signal.
numbers: 38 real hardware failures: hypothesis quality 95.6%, Pass@1 fix rate 71.1%, Pass@5 86.8%. Minimum of 3 narratives; hypotheses with confidence below 0.2 after three iterations are marked, not dropped.
quote: This adaptive approach prevents premature pruning of potentially critical failure paths.
limits: No ablation of the keep-all-hypotheses rule; hypothesis quality judged by LLM metrics; domain-specific.
agent_relevance: A concrete data structure for the hypothesis list: store confidence and the unexplored frontier per hypothesis, demote but do not delete. Fits our rule that code holds the list.

source: Berner, Jackson, Algina (1996) Relationships among performance scores of four diagnostic decision support systems (JAMIA)
finding: Older knowledge-base diagnostic programs were scored on 105 cases each. Whether the correct diagnosis was produced was not related to how many diagnoses the program listed. Having the disease in the knowledge base mattered.
numbers: 4 systems (DXplain, Iliad, Meditel, QMR), 105 cases each, 7 performance scores. Correct-diagnosis scores (top ten and full list) were linked to knowledge-base coverage and comprehensiveness.
quote: The production of a correct diagnosis for a given case is not related to the number of diagnoses suggested by the DDSS.
limits: Abstract-level page only; no percentages or list lengths. Quote as returned from the summarised page.
agent_relevance: Longer hypothesis lists did not buy accuracy in classical systems; coverage of the right hypotheses did. For LLMs, breadth helps only if the generator can reach the true cause.

source: Miller, Pople, Myers (1982) INTERNIST-1, an experimental computer-based diagnostic consultant for general internal medicine (NEJM)
finding: INTERNIST-1 ranked diseases from findings and handled several diseases by scoring a set. On 19 NEJM clinicopathological cases it looked similar to hospital clinicians but below the case discussants.
numbers: 19 CPC cases (search snippet only).
limits: Not opened; snippet only.
agent_relevance: Early AI system built on hypothesis lists and scoring. Its stated weak spots (no anatomic or temporal reasoning) still show up in LLM failure lists.

source: Pokharel, Dantu (2026) Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
finding: Each LLM agent in a group has a hidden belief (an anchor) that keeps pulling its answers during deliberation. When the anchor is far from the starting opinions, confidence in the correct answer can rise beyond what any agent first held, which classical consensus rules forbid.
numbers: Three open model families, disease-classification task. Runs escaping the initial belief hull: Llama about 77% (mean overshoot 0.22); Qwen and gpt-oss about 25%. Llama dynamic-family accuracy 43%.
limits: Opinion-dynamics model, not human diagnosis; numbers read from fragmented PDF text, so approximate. Not tied to hypothesis count.
agent_relevance: Weak link only: the model's own prior acts as a fixed pull even when others give feedback, so group chat does not clear it (G9).

source: A Mechanistic View of Authority Hierarchy in LLM Sycophancy (2026)
finding: A wrong hint from a more authoritative persona lowered accuracy more. A board-certified physician persona hurt most.
numbers: From search snippet only: Llama-3.1-8B from about 60% to 15%, Qwen to 29%, Gemma to 34%. Not verified.
limits: Not opened; snippet only.
agent_relevance: Suggested diagnoses stamped with authority are the strongest anchors. Strip authorship and status from any hypothesis before the agent tests it (G5).

source: Randomized trial of physician automation bias with erroneous ChatGPT-4o suggestions and a confidence nudge (2026)
finding: Physicians shown deliberately wrong LLM diagnoses did worse than controls. A nudge showing the model's baseline accuracy and a colour-coded confidence signal reduced the effect.
numbers: From search snippets only: treatment arm 73.3% vs control 84.9% (adjusted -14.0 points); nudge arm +7.6 points (95% CI 1.4-13.9, p=0.016). Which snippet belongs to which report is not confirmed.
limits: Not opened; snippet only; attribution of the two results uncertain.
agent_relevance: Supplying a hypothesis can harm the reader when it is wrong. Our agent should treat an inserted hypothesis as a candidate to falsify and show its track record.
